story.logline: Walk the newspaper's civil rights files from 1954 to 1965 and put the true story back.

progressEffects.before: EVENTS RAN IN CHAPTER ORDER · UNVERIFIED
OLD PAPERS ARE PRIMARY SOURCES · UNVERIFIED

restoredLine.text: Every light on the Engine is on. The whole record is back.
Every light on the Engine is on. The whole record is back.

approach.text: These three slides are all about Brown v. Board, the 1954 school case. The storm slipped one false slide in.

instruction.text: Point the lamp at the false slide, then pull it out.

tutorial.text: The lamp shows whichever slide you point it at. The FILE card shows when each slide says things happened.

insight.text: Each slide makes a claim about a time. Check those times on the FILE card.

hints.text: The ruling came in 1954. Ask what schools really looked like a few years after that.
Check each slide against Little Rock in 1957, pinned on the RECORD card. Nine students needed soldiers to get in.
The slide about Plessy and 'separate but equal' is true. Compare the other two.

default.text: That slide is true. Look for the one about what schools did after the ruling.

line.text: Brown really did end 'separate but equal,' so that slide is true. The false one is about what came after.

success.text: That's it. Brown changed the law in 1954, but schools took years to follow it.

payoffLine.text: The steps are back! Climb them to get past the water, Nell.

after.text: The plaque by the door just lit. It quotes the ruling word for word.

approach.text: The street by the bus stop is flooded. These planks tell the story of the Montgomery bus boycott.

instruction.text: Lay the planks across the road in the order they happened.

tutorial.text: Each plank turns into a slab where you drop it. Drag the year slider, and the DAY counter counts along.

insight.text: A boycott means people stop using something to protest. Here, people walked instead of riding the bus.

hints.text: Start with the arrest on December 1, 1955. Everything else grew out of that day.
Nobody walks for 381 days without a plan. Ask what had to happen before the long walk.
The plank about Parks acting all alone never happened. She was part of a group ready to act.

default.text: The road won't hold there. The boycott had to be planned before 381 days of walking.

line.text: That slab sank. Nobody runs a year-long boycott alone, so that plank never happened.

success.text: One arrest became a 381-day boycott because people planned it. It ended when the Supreme Court ruled.

payoffLine.text: Walk it, Nell. That's 381 days, one slab at a time.

after.text: The bus lights are on. Those seats were what all that walking was for.

approach.text: It's September 1957. The state's National Guard is blocking nine Black students at the school door.

instruction.text: Turn the knob to your guess, then send it down the wire.

tutorial.text: The ticker types your guess as you turn the knob. Nothing goes out until you send it.

insight.text: A federal court ordered the school to let the students in. The governor is ignoring that order.

hints.text: The governor is ignoring an order from a federal court. That's the fight here.
Ask who has more power than a governor when a federal court is ignored. Check each choice against that.
Canceling the order would mean the governor won. That's not what happened, so compare the other two.

default.text: The wire prints what really happened. Read it, then turn the knob to that outcome and send it.

line.text: The tape says no. When a state ignores a federal court, the choice is out of Arkansas's hands.

success.text: Brown didn't enforce itself. When a governor ignored a federal court, it took the President and the Army.

payoffLine.text: Nine lamps, one for each student who walked in.

after.text: Those doors stay open now. Go on through, Nell.

approach.text: Someone swapped the menu for three slides about the Greensboro sit-ins. One of them is lying.

instruction.text: Swing the counter lamp onto the lying slide, then pull it out.

tutorial.text: The lamp swings to whichever slide you pick. It only pulls one out when you say so.

insight.text: At a sit-in, people sat where they weren't allowed and wouldn't leave. That took a lot of planning.

hints.text: Sitting at a counter where you're banned is already a challenge to the rules.
Nonviolent means you don't hit back. Which slide fits students who broke a rule on purpose?
The slide about February 1, 1960 is true. Compare the other two.

default.text: That slide is true. Look for the one that makes nonviolent sound like doing nothing.

line.text: That one's true, since the sit-ins really did spread. Look for the claim about how the students acted.

success.text: Right! The students broke an unfair rule on purpose. They stayed calm, even when people hurt them.

payoffLine.text: The kitchen door's open. The alley leads to the bus station.

approach.text: The bus station's power line is dead. Six boxes hold events from 1961, and one doesn't belong.

instruction.text: Wire each junction box to the event it caused, then close the circuit.

tutorial.text: Draw a wire from a box to what it caused. The gauge only counts wires, so it can't tell you if they're right.

insight.text: The Freedom Riders rode buses together to see if a new ruling would be obeyed.

hints.text: The riders got on the buses to test something. Find the event they were testing.
Look for what turned the Anniston attack into news across the country. That link comes right after the attack.
Congress passed no civil rights law in 1961, so leave that box out. Kennedy's push comes last.

default.text: The power stops at that box. Follow the pressure, and ask who acted last.

line.text: Congress passed no such law in 1961. The riders didn't wait for one.

success.text: Riders tested a ruling, and the attack made headlines. Only then did Washington act.

payoffLine.text: The gate's up. Take the stairs up to the overpass.

approach.text: Five stations go up the mast, plus one that doesn't belong. Link each Birmingham event to the one it caused.

instruction.text: Wire the relay stations up the mast, cause to effect, then close the circuit.

tutorial.text: Each dish turns toward whatever you wire into it. The lift at the bottom stays dark until the circuit closes.

insight.text: A bill is a plan for a new law. Kennedy's came after a lot of people started pushing.

hints.text: Everything starts with the marches in Birmingham. Ask what happened to the marchers next.
The pictures only mattered once people saw them. Find what came after TV and the newspapers.
The Voting Rights Act station is from 1965, so it doesn't fit this spring. Kennedy's bill is the last link.

default.text: The signal dies partway up. Ask what people had to see before anyone in Washington acted.

line.text: That station is from 1965. This mast only covers Birmingham in the spring of 1963, and that June.

success.text: Kennedy's bill had a chain of causes. Marches met violence, and cameras made the whole country see it.

payoffLine.text: The lift's working. Ride it up to the rooftops.

after.text: You can see the whole city from up here. Those TV pictures reached every city in the country.

document.title: MARCH ON WASHINGTON FOR JOBS AND FREEDOM · AUGUST 28, 1963

approach.text: The march's program is scrambled on the switchboard. There are four names and five parts, so one part is extra.

instruction.text: Plug each name jack into its role jack, then connect the program.

tutorial.text: Plug in a cord and both lamps turn white. White just means plugged in, and it doesn't check the match.

insight.text: A crowd of 250,000 people takes months of planning before anyone gives a speech.

hints.text: The march's full name was the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. One part matches those words.
Randolph and Rustin were both organizers. One had the idea years earlier, and one ran the day itself.
Nobody at the march signed the Civil Rights Act into law. A president did that the next year.

default.text: That cord won't stay in. Labor and civil rights leaders planned this march, so check the program's edge.

line.text: King gave the last speech. The call for this march came years earlier, from a labor leader.

success.text: A big team planned this march, and it asked for jobs as well as freedom. King's famous speech closed the day.

payoffLine.text: The steps are solid. Climb up to the columns, Nell.

after.text: The program printed clean. Look, the famous speech is only the last line.

approach.text: Two cabinets for two laws, and six slips coming down the tube. Each slip is one part of a law.

instruction.text: File each slip in the cabinet for its law, then seal the cabinets.

tutorial.text: Each slip flies to the drawer you pick. The meters only count slips, and they don't check your filing.

insight.text: These two laws came one year apart. Each one fixed a different unfair thing.

hints.text: Each slip is about daily life and jobs, or about voting. That decides the cabinet.
Try the slip about restaurants and hotels. It's about public places, so ask which law covered those.
Two slips only give dates, July 1964 and March 1965. Match each to the year in a law's name.

default.text: A slip bounced back. The 1964 law fought segregation and unfair hiring, and voting waited for 1965.

line.text: Something about voting is sitting with the 1964 act. Read the label on that cabinet again.

success.text: The 1964 act opened lunch counters, hotels and workplaces. Voting needed its own law a year later.

payoffLine.text: The cabinets rolled apart. There's a stairway down to the river road.

approach.text: This chapter tells things out of order. Go by the dates.
The bridge deck is in pieces. Set the planks by their dates, and leave out the one from another story.

instruction.text: Set the bridge planks in date order, then lock the bridge.

tutorial.text: The planks come in the order the chapter prints them. Each part of the deck shows its plank's date.

insight.text: A textbook tells events in the order that makes a good chapter. The dates show the real order.

hints.text: Go by the dates on the planks. The page order in the chapter doesn't count.
Start with the plank from 1964. The rest of this story happened in 1965.
The December 1956 plank is from the bus boycott, so leave it out. Then sort the two March planks by day.

default.text: The bridge tips there. Drag the year slider across the bridge and watch which lamps light up.

line.text: That plank is dated 1956. It's from the Montgomery bus story.

success.text: Yes! The dates set the order. The 1964 act came first, and the 1965 act came after Selma.

payoffLine.text: The bridge holds, and the rain's stopping. Walk across slowly, Nell.

after.text: The plate on the far bank is lit. Read it before the streetcar takes us home.

approach.text: Six documents spilled out of the cabinet. Theo thinks anything old counts as a primary source.

instruction.text: File each document in the Primary or Secondary drawer, then seal the stacks.

tutorial.text: Each document gets a date stamp when it lands. It shows the year it was made.

insight.text: A primary source was made at the time by someone who was there. A secondary one was made later.

hints.text: Look at who made each document and when. How old it is doesn't decide it.
Test the 2019 film about Selma. Its makers weren't there, so they learned it from older sources.
The 1963 photo and the 1971 textbook are both old. Only one was made by someone at the march.

default.text: That drawer spat it back. Check who made this, and whether they were there when it happened.

line.text: The textbook went in Primary because it looks old. Its writer wasn't there, and that's the test.

success.text: A source is primary because of who made it and when. A 1971 textbook is still secondhand.

payoffLine.text: The stacks are rolling apart. The ladder to the balcony is free.

approach.text: This is the Big Board. Link Birmingham to the Voting Rights Act, and leave out two canisters from an earlier story.

instruction.text: Run a tube from each event to the one it caused, then send the capsule.

tutorial.text: Tubes grow along the board as you draw them. The RECORD card has every date you've fixed so far.

insight.text: Every pin on the RECORD card is a date. Use them to check each link.

hints.text: Start with the TV pictures from Birmingham in May 1963. End with the vote in August 1965.
Each new law came after the country saw violence on TV. Find the crisis before each law.
Brown in 1954 and Montgomery in 1955 are too early for this chain. Leave them out.

default.text: The capsule got stuck. Each tube needs a cause and what it led to, so check the RECORD card's dates.

line.text: Brown and Montgomery matter, but they're part of an earlier story. This board runs from Birmingham to the vote.

success.text: Birmingham led to the 1964 act, and Selma led to the 1965 act. Both laws came after the country saw violence on TV.

payoffLine.text: The Big Board's lit, and the vault's first bolt just moved. The Editor is waiting for you, Nell.

approach.text: Each tumbler holds one explanation. Pin each clue to the one it rules out until one is left.

instruction.text: Pin clues to the tumblers they rule out, then pick the explanation that's left.

tutorial.text: Your strike marks are just for you, and the vault never reads them. It only opens for the answer you pick.

insight.text: A good explanation fits every dated clue. One clue against it is enough to strike it.

hints.text: Start with the clue about the 2% of Black adults signed up to vote in early 1965.
If under 2% could vote after the 1964 act, that act hadn't fixed voting. Strike that tumbler.
The court clue rules out one more. Then test the explanation about Brown against the March 15, 1965 clue.

default.text: One of your own clues rules that one out. Find the clue card next to that row.

success.text: Yes! TV pictures of Selma pushed a voting bill forward in days. Eleven years of waiting hadn't done that.

fail.text: That tumbler won't turn. One of your own clues rules it out.
Dead end. A dated clue already ruled that out.

lines.text: Go to the courthouse first, Nell. Wick knows the way.
I'll try to keep this floor dry. Stay close to that lantern.
From up here, the square looks like a front page. The water goes all the way to the bus stop.

plaques.title: Brown v. Board of Education (1954)
plaques.text: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954) the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.

sourceRef.quote: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954) the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.

plaques.title: Little Rock Nine (1957)
plaques.text: President Eisenhower responded by sending soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students into the school.

sourceRef.quote: President Eisenhower responded by sending soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students into the school.

plaques.title: Anniston, Alabama (1961)
plaques.text: In Anniston, Alabama, a mob firebombed one of the buses and beat the riders as they escaped.

sourceRef.quote: In Anniston, Alabama, a mob firebombed one of the buses and beat the riders as they escaped.

plaques.title: The Edmund Pettus Bridge, 1965
plaques.text: On March 7, 1965, state troopers attacked peaceful marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, a day remembered as Bloody Sunday.

sourceRef.quote: On March 7, 1965, state troopers attacked peaceful marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, a day remembered as Bloody Sunday.

lines.text: Watch out for the water. The storm got in through the windows and soaked the film reels.
The files run from 1954 to 1965. Walk the years in order.
That big machine turns the paper's old news into a city you can walk.
Some steps go nowhere, and false labels cover the true ones.
Put each true story back, and the next year will open.
The last vault asks why the voting law passed. It opens when the rest of the story is true.
My knees can't do the walking anymore. Take Wick, and he'll carry my voice.
Start at the courthouse. The story begins with a court ruling, and what people did after it.
The main switch is by the Engine. The water hit the other fuses, but the Engine has its own line.
Flip the main switch by the Engine, Nell. We'll see what still works.
There she goes. Haven't seen those rings turn since the week I was hired.
If a fix doesn't hold, the Engine shows you where. Watch for it, Nell.
You found the story I locked away. People pushed for years, and that's how the laws passed.
People kept telling it as one speech and one signature. Really, it took years of organizing.
Look out the window, Nell. The whole city is back, from 1954 to 1965.
Every event is linked to what caused it now. You can back up this record with proof.
Sun's up. Nobody's hauling anything out of here today.
Front page is set. First edition in ten minutes.
Go home and get some sleep. If anyone asks what happened, tell them why it happened too.
This is Courthouse Square in 1954. The record is mixed up about what the Court decided.
This is Little Rock in September 1957. Three years after Brown, those school doors are still shut.
This is Greensboro in 1960, with a bus station next door. Young people are leading the protests now.
Now we're in Birmingham, spring 1963. What happened here mattered because TV cameras showed it.
Washington, August 1963. Getting 250,000 people here took a huge amount of planning.
This is Selma in March 1965. The bridge is in pieces, so we'll set them by date.
We're back in the stacks. The rest of the record is papers, and what caused what.
Here's my question. Why did the voting law pass in 1965?
